supported_claims.text: 上 is an indicative graph: a short mark above a longer reference line indicates “above” or “upper side.” The sources describe early reference lines differently—as curved in some forms or as horizontal—while agreeing on the positional marking.

The earliest reported uses include Shang-period contexts such as 上帝 and 上甲, as well as contrasts with 下. Spatial uses meaning “above” and “at/on the side of” are reported for Zhou bronze inscriptions.

Later graphic accounts describe the upper mark becoming vertical to distinguish 上 from 二; the modern standard form is described as adding a dot. These are graphic changes, separate from the character’s meanings.

Reported uses include “more than,” and later literary uses include “ruler,” “elder,” or someone in authority. The dossier does not establish a dated sequence connecting these uses to the spatial meaning, or a precise chronology for “ascend” and “send up.”

The received Shuowen analysis treats 丄 as an ancient form meaning “high” and labels it indicative, but this is evidence for a Han-era account rather than independent confirmation of the earlier graphic history. The dossier also records an editorial difference over whether the received head form is 丄 or 二.

disagreements.text: Accounts agree that an upper mark sits above a reference line, but differ on whether the earliest line was curved or horizontal. No primary inscription image was inspected here to resolve the variation.

limitations.text: The earliest graph form discussed in the dossier is oracle-bone 上; no earlier dated occurrence of this specific graph is established here. This is a limit of the dossier, not a claim that the character’s origin is unknown.

Inscriptional examples and their dates are reported by secondary paleographic sources; the named artifacts were generally not independently checked. The Shang bone photograph’s transcription includes 上甲, but its description does not isolate the 上 graph.
The dossier proposes no semantic or phonetic components. It analyzes the graph as indicative, so no component sound comparison is applicable.
The dossier does not establish a dated semantic progression to “superior,” “ruler,” or verbal “ascend/send up”; gloss order alone does not establish such development.
